operations.old: SBONEST fits decoupling sidebands in heteronuclear chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST), including ¹⁵N and ¹³C profiles described by an isolated XH spin pair. We use a 30 ppm ¹⁵N window at a proton frequency of 1.2 GHz as the quantitative benchmark. Although high-power composite pulse decoupling can suppress these artifacts, its use over a long saturation period is constrained by probe power handling and sample heating. When sidebands persist under the available RF conditions, quantitative fitting must account for the coupled XH dynamics. SBONEST propagates the applied proton pulse train explicitly. On the same noisy synthetic profiles, conventional nitrogen-only fitting gives χ²/dof=67.95 and kex=321.4 s⁻¹, whereas SBONEST gives 0.968 and 300.2 s⁻¹ for a generating rate of 300 s⁻¹. The conventional fit also lowers minor-state R2N from the generating 15.0 to 7.80 s⁻¹, compared with 15.22 s⁻¹ for SBONEST. The rate displacement persists without noise. Repeated 90x–240y–90x decoupling with a 70 μs 90° pulse has a nominal first-sideband separation of 1530.6 Hz, corresponding to 25.18, 18.88 and 12.59 ppm on ¹⁵N at 600 MHz, 800 MHz and 1.2 GHz, respectively. We combine this geometry with a coupled NH exchange model implemented in SBONEST. In independent simulations sampled uniformly across 105–135 ppm at approximately 25 Hz spacing, retaining sideband regions at 1.2 GHz reduced local standard errors of the nitrogen RF scale and minor-state population by 19.1% and 17.1%, whereas the exchange-rate improvement was 1.8%. Stock-pulse calculations imported from cestdec and independently checked here explain the RF dependence and offset shifts of the sidebands. These results support a conditional improvement in the use of already acquired data, rather than a general advantage in information per unit time. We specify experiments to test the effect of field, pulse timing, RF calibration and sampling phase. A separate noiseless ¹³C–¹H configuration test recovers all eight generating parameters. Experimental validation remains prospective.

operations.old: The noise-free 1.2 GHz fit recovered all eight parameters, with reduced χ²=1.38×10⁻¹⁹. For noisy data, the full fit gave kex=300.224 s⁻¹, pB=4.9946% and ν₁N scale=1.08138, with reduced χ²=0.9679. The masked fit gave 300.316 s⁻¹, 4.9896% and 1.08205, respectively. Both fits had full Jacobian rank and no parameters at a bound. Thus, in this noise realization both recovered the exchange process; the main distinction is the uncertainty, not a dramatic shift in the point estimates.

operations.old: Fitting the full sideband-containing profiles with the nitrogen-only model gives χ²/dof=67.95, compared with 0.968 for the coupled NH model on the identical observations (Table 5; Figure 5). The largest absolute standardized residual is approximately 109 for the nitrogen-only fit, versus 2.80 for SBONEST. The nitrogen-only model cannot reproduce the decoupling dips and compensates by shifting the parameters that govern the central and exchange responses: kex rises from the generating 300 s⁻¹ to 321.4 s⁻¹ (+7.13%), pB falls from 5.000% to 4.812%, and the RF scale rises from 1.080 to 1.0958. The fitted minor-state R2N also falls from 15.0 to 7.80 s⁻¹. SBONEST instead recovers kex=300.2 s⁻¹, pB=4.995%, RF scale=1.0814 and minor-state R2N=15.22 s⁻¹. These are deviations for one noise realization, not ensemble estimates of bias.

operations.old: Excluding the prespecified sideband regions improves the nitrogen-only fit to χ²/dof=3.726, but kex remains 321.2 s⁻¹ and pB becomes 4.710%. The same masked observations fitted with the NH model give χ²/dof=0.999 and kex=300.3 s⁻¹. Thus, this particular mask removes the prominent sideband regions without making the retained profiles equivalent to perfect proton decoupling. It does not establish that every possible mask would fail. The noiseless nitrogen-only fits return kex=321.1 s⁻¹ for the full grid and 320.8 s⁻¹ for the masked grid, confirming a deterministic displacement of the optimum in this example. The legacy zero-clipping convention gives χ²/dof=67.950 and 3.732 for the noisy full and masked fits, respectively, and does not account for the model discrepancy. Formal covariance errors from the misspecified model should not be interpreted as validated confidence intervals.

All fitted estimates are reported with one local standard error (estimate ± 1 SE). At each fitted parameter vector, J is the Jacobian of residuals divided by their supplied intensity errors, and C=(JᵀJ)⁻¹ is evaluated by singular-value decomposition. SEᵢ=√Cᵢᵢ; C is not multiplied by χ²/dof. For kex=kAB+kBA, pB=kAB/kex and δB=δA+Δδ, we use SE(g)=√(∇gᵀC∇g), including cross-covariances. Population SE values accompanying percentages are in percentage points. These fitted-point SE values differ from the generating-point information estimates in Table 4. For misspecified nitrogen-only models, they quantify within-model local curvature and exclude model discrepancy; they are not validated confidence intervals. Noiseless checks retain the assigned σ=0.001 weights, so their nonzero SE describes hypothetical measurement noise, not observed replicate scatter. Known generating values and fixed inputs have no fitted SE.
